I always wonder why we still have to keep track of the epoch in order to compute time.

Because not only is an integer the smallest way to store dates, it makes it much easier to convert timezones. There are databases maintained to convert epochs into timezones, including DST rules: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tz_database

You have to include DST rules, half-timezones and quarter-timezones, date changes (part of Kiribati skipped an entire day when it moved across the date line)... such a thing gets messy:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-5wpm-gesOY

Keeping track of time as a single number is pretty efficient for most purposes(temporal arithmetic is fairly common). The alternative is to keep track of every single piece of time separately, which is only helpful for display purposes(perhaps the rarest thing ever done with a time). The concept of "epoch" only exists because time is very much a mixed radix thing, so you're inherently left with a relative time when converting it to a flat number and need to decide what it's all relative to; midnight January 1st, AD 1 might seem the most logical choice but 1970 was far more practical.
